interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a square of pinned bars folding flat and a triangle keeping its shape, until one diagonal bar locks the square, when you drag a joint.
interactive.title: The frame on two supports
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in fifteen small screens about a frame of bars. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each bar is a straight line between two joints. Each joint is a ring you can drag. The joints are pins, free to turn like hinges. The frame stands on two supports. A pin support under the left foot can push any way. A roller under the right foot can only push straight up. A counter compares the frame's bars with 2j − 3, where j is the number of joints. A load can hang from any joint. The supports' pushes then appear as arrows, each with its size. Tap a joint to draw its forces nose to tail beside the frame. Each bar's arrow at that pin is labelled pull or push. Here is the rule the picture follows. A bar fixes the distance between its two pins and nothing else. With fewer than 2j − 3 bars, each placed where it locks something, a frame still has a way to move, and the drag folds it. Under a load, every joint is in balance, so its forces drawn nose to tail close up. Each bar pushes or pulls only along its own length. The supports' pushes come from taking moments about one support for the whole frame. A readout that would give a puzzle's answer shows "?" until the answer is checked. Any row of readouts wraps onto two lines on a phone. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, Which holds?: a square frame and a triangle frame of pinned bars side by side, each standing on a pin support and a roller, with a hand arrow pushing sideways at the top of each. "Push sideways on the top of each frame. Which one keeps its shape?" Choices, in a column: The triangle (right); The square; Both keep their shape; Neither keeps its shape. Read: "A square frame and a triangle frame of pinned bars each stand on two supports. Push sideways on the top of each. Which one keeps its shape?" Why: every joint is a pin, free to turn like a hinge. The square's four bars can all lean over into a diamond. So the square folds. Three bars of fixed length make one triangle and no other. So the triangle cannot change shape. After Check, both frames are pushed. The square folds flat. The triangle holds. Screen 2, show, Triangles hold: both frames again, the square folded over. Words: "A pin lets bars turn at a joint, like a hinge. So a bar fixes only the distance between its two pins. Three fixed lengths make one triangle and no other. So a triangle of pinned bars is rigid. Four fixed lengths can make a square or a thin diamond. So a square folds." Then "Drag any joint." Read: "When one joint is dragged, the square leans over until it folds flat. The triangle's joints will not move." Screen 3, show, Counting ways to move: the triangle and the square, with a counter under each reading its bars against 2j − 3. Words: "On a flat page, each joint can move two ways, across and up. So j joints have 2j ways to move. Three of those ways slide or turn the whole frame without changing its shape. Each bar can stop one of the rest. So a frame of j joints needs at least 2j − 3 bars to hold its shape." Then "Tap the triangle, then the square." Read: "The triangle has 3 joints and 3 bars. It needs 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so it holds. The square has 4 joints and 4 bars. It needs 2 × 4 − 3 = 5, so it is one short and folds." Screen 4, do, typed, Lock the frame: a square frame with a triangle roof on top, 5 joints and 6 bars, on its two supports, its counter showing "?". "This frame is a square with a roof on top. It has 5 joints. What is the fewest bars it needs to hold its shape?" A typed answer: 7 bars, a whole number. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 6 bars, 10 bars, 5 bars. Hint: "Use 2j − 3, with j the number of joints." Read: "A square frame with a triangle roof on top has 5 joints and 6 bars. What is the fewest bars it needs to hold its shape?" Why: it needs 2 × 5 − 3 = 7 bars. It has only 6. So it has one way left to move, and its square part leans over. A diagonal across the square is the seventh bar. Then the whole frame is triangles. After Check, the diagonal appears. Dragging a joint no longer moves the frame. The counter shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 5, do, typed, Grow the frame: two square bays side by side on the supports, with a diagonal in the left bay only, the right bay leaning. "This frame has 6 joints and 8 bars. How many more bars does it need to hold its shape?" A typed answer: 1 bar, a whole number. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 4 bars, 9 bars, 0 bars. Hint: "Work out 2j − 3. Then take away the 8 bars it has." Read: "A frame of two square bays has 6 joints and 8 bars. How many more bars does it need to hold its shape?" Why: it needs 2 × 6 − 3 = 9 bars. It has 8, so it needs 1 more. That is a diagonal across the right bay. Each new joint brings two ways to move, so it needs two new bars. That is why a frame grown one triangle at a time keeps the count right. After Check, the second diagonal appears. The right bay locks. Screen 6, show, The supports push back: the triangle frame, its sloping bars at 30° to level, the pin support under its left foot and the roller under its right foot. Words: "Hang a load on a joint, and the supports push back. Find those pushes first. Treat the whole frame as one body. Take moments about one support, as for a mobile's bar. The pin can push any way. The roller can only push straight up." Then "Tap a joint to hang the load there." Read: "A 10 kN load hangs from the top joint, midway between the supports. Each support pushes up with 5 kN." Screen 7, do, typed, Off centre: a longer frame of five triangles on the supports, 6 m between them, with 4 joints along the bottom 2 m apart and 3 along the top. A 12 kN load hangs from the bottom joint 2 m from the left support. The reaction arrows show "?". "A frame spans 6 m between its supports. A 12 kN load hangs from a joint 2 m from the left support. How hard does the left support push up?" A typed answer: 8 kN, a whole number. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 4 kN, 6 kN. Hint: "Take moments about the right support." Why: the load is 6 − 2 = 4 m from the right support. Its moment about that support is 12 × 4 = 48 kN m. The left support is 6 m away, and its push must balance that moment. So it pushes 48 ÷ 6 = 8 kN. The right support takes the rest, 12 − 8 = 4 kN. The supports' pushes show "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 8, show, Pull or push: one bar between two pins, with an arrow at each pin. Words: "Each bar in a loaded frame is pulled or pushed along its length. Look at its arrow at a pin. If it points away from the pin, the bar pulls. It is in tension. If it points into the pin, the bar pushes. It is in compression." Then "Drag one pin to stretch or squash the bar." Read: "A stretched bar pulls its pins towards each other. So its arrow at each pin points away from that pin, labelled pull. A squashed bar pushes its pins apart. So each arrow points into its pin, labelled push." Screen 9, do, Which is pulled?: the triangle frame from screen 6 with its 10 kN load at the top joint, the bar arrows hidden. "A triangle frame carries a load at its top joint. Which bar is in tension?" Choices, in a column: The bottom bar (right); The two sloping bars; All three bars; None of them. Why: the load presses the top joint down. That squashes both sloping bars. Squashed, they push their feet outwards. The roller cannot push sideways. So the bottom bar holds the feet together by pulling. After Check, every bar shows its arrows and its pull or push label. Screen 10, show, Joint by joint: the same frame and load, with the top joint's three forces drawn nose to tail beside it. Words: "The forces at each joint balance. So, drawn nose to tail, they close into a triangle. A joint's balance gives two equations, across and up. So it can find two unknowns. Start at a joint with only two unknown bars, like the top joint. The bars slope equally, so each up part holds half the load, 5 kN. That up part is the bar's force × sin 30°. So each bar pushes with 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 kN." Then "Tap the top joint." Read: "At the top joint, the 10 kN load and the bars' two 10 kN pushes close into a triangle with three equal sides. Both bar arrows point into the pin, so both are in compression." Screen 11, do, typed, The bottom bar: the left foot of the same frame, with the support's 5 kN push up, the sloping bar's 10 kN push into the foot, and the bottom bar's force showing "?". "At the left foot, the support pushes up with 5 kN. The sloping bar pushes into the foot with 10 kN, at 30° above level. What is the force in the bottom bar?" A typed answer: 8.66 kN, to two decimal places. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 10 kN, 5 kN, 11.55 kN. Hint: "Balance the across parts at the foot." Why: the sloping bar's across part is 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 kN. It pushes the foot outwards. Its up part is 10 × sin 30° = 5 kN, which matches the support's push. The pin could push sideways too. But no other force on the frame pushes sideways, so here it pushes only up. So the bottom bar must pull the foot inwards with 8.66 kN. Its arrow points away from the pin, so it is in tension. The force shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 12, show, A screw is a ramp: a screw whose thread unrolls, one turn at a time, into a ramp, its climb drawn five times taller. Words: "A screw's thread is a ramp wrapped round a shaft. Laid flat, one turn runs the screw's circumference, π × 20 = 62.8 mm. It climbs one pitch, the gap between threads, here 2 mm. With friction ignored, the work in equals the work out. So push × 62.8 mm = load × 2 mm, and the load is 31.4 times the push." Then "Play the unrolling." Read: "One turn of a 20 mm screw's thread unrolls into a ramp 62.8 mm long. The ramp climbs 2 mm, drawn five times taller here. With friction ignored, a push along the thread lifts a load 31.4 times its size." Still: the thread fully unrolled. Screen 13, do, typed, A finer thread: the same 20 mm screw with a 1.5 mm pitch, still wound, and "load lifted ÷ push = ?" under it. "The same 20 mm screw gets a finer thread, with a 1.5 mm pitch. With friction ignored, how many times the push is the load?" A typed answer: 41.9 times, to one decimal place. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 31.4, 13.3, 94.2. Hint: "Divide one turn's length, 62.8 mm, by its climb." Why: one turn runs π × 20 = 62.8 mm and climbs 1.5 mm. So push × 62.8 mm = load × 1.5 mm. The load is 62.8 ÷ 1.5 = 41.9 times the push. A finer thread lifts more for each push, but takes more turns. That is how a terminal screw clamps a conductor hard from a small twist. Left loose, it presses on less of the conductor, and the joint runs hot. After Check, the thread unrolls into a ramp 62.8 mm long that climbs 1.5 mm, and the sum reads 62.8 ÷ 1.5 = 41.9. Screen 14, do, mixed, Same count: two frames of two square bays each. Frame A has a diagonal in each bay. Frame B has both diagonals crossed in its left bay and none in its right. "Both frames have 6 joints and 9 bars, as 2j − 3 asks. Which one folds?" Choices, in a column: Frame B, both diagonals in one bay (right); Frame A, a diagonal in each bay; Neither, since both have 9 bars; Both of them. Read: "Two frames of two square bays each have 6 joints and 9 bars. Frame A has a diagonal in each bay. Frame B has both diagonals in its left bay. Which one folds?" Why: the count says how many bars a frame needs, not where they go. Frame B's second diagonal locks nothing the first one had not already locked. So it is spare. Its right bay is a square with no diagonal, so it folds. After Check, Frame B's right bay leans over. Screen 15, do, mixed, typed, A steeper frame: a triangle frame on the two supports, its sloping bars at 45° to level, a 12 kN load at its top joint, each sloping bar's force showing "?". "A triangle frame on two supports carries 12 kN at its top joint. Its sloping bars are at 45° to level. What force is in each sloping bar?" A typed answer: 8.49 kN, to two decimal places. Slips, each with a hint naming its mistake: 6 kN, 12 kN, 4.24 kN. Hint: "Each sloping bar's up part holds half the load." Why: the two bars slope equally, so they share the load equally. Each bar's up part is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN. The up part is the force × sin 45°. So the force is 6 ÷ 0.707 = 8.49 kN. Both arrows point into the top joint, so both bars are in compression. At each foot, the bottom bar then pulls with 8.49 × cos 45° = 6.00 kN. The forces show "?" until the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: The bars are drawn weightless. Every load hangs at a joint. The pins turn with no friction. Most real frames are bolted or welded. So their joints resist turning a little. Their bars also bend a little, as well as stretching or squashing. The bars stretch and squash too little to see, so the picture keeps their lengths fixed. Nothing here breaks. A long, thin bar in compression can bow sideways. It can then fail well below the force that would crush it. The picture does not show that. Everything is drawn flat. A real frame also needs bracing across its width. The screw has a single thread, so one turn moves it one pitch. Its friction is left out. Its climb is drawn five times taller than it is. Real screws lose a good part of the push to friction. Every load, length and angle is an example figure, not taken from a real frame.

explain.text:
A frame of bars joined by pins holds its shape when it is built from triangles. Put a load on it, and each bar is either pulled or pushed along its length. Balancing the forces at each joint in turn tells you which, and how hard.

Start with why triangles hold. A pin lets the bars turn at a joint, like a hinge. So a bar fixes only one thing, the distance between its two pins. Three fixed lengths make one triangle and no other. So a triangle of three pinned bars is rigid. Four fixed lengths can make a square or a thin diamond. So a square folds. You can count this. On a flat page, each joint can move two ways, across and up. So j joints have 2j ways to move. Three of those ways move the whole frame without changing its shape. They are two slides and a turn, and the supports stop them. Each of the other ways changes the shape. Each bar can stop one of them. Each way left to move is a [[degree of freedom]]. A frame with one left can fold. So a frame needs at least 2j − 3 bars to hold its shape. A simple frame is grown one triangle at a time. It has exactly m = 2j − 3, where m is the number of bars.[^1] A square has 4 joints, so it needs 5 bars. With only 4, it has a degree of freedom left. A diagonal as the fifth bar locks it. The count tells you how many bars, not where they go. Each one must lock something, as a diagonal does when it splits a square into two triangles.

Now the forces. First, find the supports' pushes. Treat the whole frame as one body. The total clockwise moment about one support equals the total anticlockwise moment about it, just as on a mobile's bar. Then go joint by joint. The count says why that works for a simple frame. Its j joints give two balance equations each, so 2j in all. Its m bars and three support pushes make m + 3 = 2j unknowns. Each joint is in balance. So its forces, drawn nose to tail, close up. Where three forces meet, they make a triangle. Start at a joint with only two unknown bars. Take a triangle frame on two supports, with its sloping bars at 30° to level. Hang 10 kN from the top joint. Each support pushes up 5 kN. At the top joint, the two sloping bars slope equally. So each one's up part holds half the load, 5 kN. That up part is the bar's force × sin 30°. So each bar carries 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 kN. At a foot, the same bar's across part is 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 kN. It pushes the foot outwards. The roller cannot push sideways. So the bottom bar must pull the feet together with 8.66 kN. To tell a pull from a push, look at the bar's arrow at the pin. If it points away from the pin, the bar is in [[tension]]. If it points into the pin, the bar is in [[compression]].[^2] Here the sloping bars push and the bottom bar pulls. Now hang the same triangle from its top joint, as two slings hang a spreader beam from a crane hook. Every force turns round. The slings pull, and the beam between their feet is squeezed. A lifting beam hangs straight from the hook at its middle. With no triangle of slings, it bends instead.

A screw is a ramp wrapped round a shaft. One turn of its thread runs the screw's circumference and climbs one pitch, the gap between threads. With friction ignored, the work in equals the work out. So the load is the push × circumference ÷ pitch.[^3] A 20 mm screw with a 2 mm pitch lifts 62.8 ÷ 2 = 31.4 times its push. A finer thread lifts more, but takes more turns. That is how a terminal screw clamps a conductor hard from a small twist. Left loose, it presses on less of the conductor, and the joint runs hot.

This is a teaching model, with weightless bars, frictionless pins and loads only at joints. Most real joints are bolted or welded. Real bars also bend a little. **A frame of pinned bars built from triangles holds its shape. Balancing the forces joint by joint shows which bars are pulled and which are pushed.**

analogy.text: Working out a frame joint by joint is like working out a circuit's branch currents node by node. At every node, the currents in equal the currents out. At every joint, the forces balance. Each balance gives an equation. With enough equations, every unknown comes out. Guess a direction for each one. If an answer comes out negative, it runs the other way. A current flows the other way round its branch. A bar pushes instead of pulls.
analogy.breaks: A node gives one equation. A current has only a size and a direction along its wire. A joint gives two, across and up, because a force can point any way on the page. A circuit also has nothing like a frame folding. A missing wire leaves a current with nowhere to flow. It does not leave a shape free to move. Node balances alone rarely settle a circuit's branch currents. You also need Ohm's law or the loop equations. In a simple frame, the joint balances alone give every bar's force.

practice.text:
- When a frame carries a real load, such as a lifting beam or a scaffold, its marked safe working load and the site's lifting plan come first. These sums explain a frame. They do not make one safe.
- Count the joints and bars. Check the bars against 2j − 3. Look for any four-sided bay with no diagonal.
- Draw the whole frame with its loads. Find the supports' pushes by taking moments about one support.
- Pick a joint with only two unknown bars. Draw its forces nose to tail. Or balance the across parts and the up parts separately.
- Solve for the two bar forces.
- Read each bar's arrow at that pin. Away from the pin is tension. Into the pin is compression.
- Move to a joint that now has only two unknowns. Repeat.
- Check the last joint. Its forces should balance with nothing left over.

**Rule of thumb:** a four-sided bay of pinned bars with no diagonal will lean over under a sideways push. In a simple triangle frame loaded at its top, the sloping bars push and the bottom bar pulls. The flatter the sloping bars, the harder they work.

**Worked example:** a triangle frame on two supports carries 20 kN at its top joint. Its sloping bars are at 60° to level. Each support pushes up 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kN. At the top joint, each sloping bar's up part holds 10 kN. So its force is 10 ÷ sin 60° = 10 ÷ 0.866 = 11.55 kN. Its arrow points into the top joint, so it is in compression. At a foot, its across part is its force × cos 60°, which is half of it. Worked from the unrounded force, that is 5.77 kN. So the bottom bar pulls with 5.77 kN. It is in tension.

**Common mistakes**
- Counting 2j bars and forgetting the three the supports take away.
- Trusting the count alone. A spare bar in one bay cannot lock another.
- Starting at a joint with three unknown bars, or before the supports' pushes are known.
- Using cos where the up part needs sin, with the angle taken from level. Or multiplying when the bar's force needs a divide.
- Reading pull or push from where an arrow sits on the drawing, rather than from which way it points at the pin.
- Letting a roller push sideways. On level ground it only pushes straight up.
